title: How to Pray for the People You Lead
subtitle: On intercession as the leader's first work, praying for your congregation by name, and why the unseen labor of prayer outranks every visible task

sections.title: The Work No One Will Ever See
sections.body:
There is a labor in ministry that earns no thanks, fills no report, and shows up in no metric. It happens before dawn or after the house is asleep, in a chair with a list of names. It is the praying, and it is the first work of the one who leads.

We will give our lives to prayer and the ministry of the word, the apostles said. They named prayer first.

They were drowning in legitimate needs, real complaints, an actual crisis in the church, and they refused to let the visible urgent work crowd out the invisible essential one. We have not kept their order. We answer the email, run the meeting, polish the sermon, and pray for our people in the cracks if at all. Then we wonder why ministry feels like pushing a stalled car uphill. It feels that way because we are doing in our own strength what was only ever meant to be done in his. The leader who does not pray for his people is not leading them. He is managing them, and they can feel the difference even when they cannot name it.

sections.title: Pray for Them by Name
sections.body:
Vague prayer for the church in general is how we avoid actually praying. Bless the congregation, we mumble, and feel we have done our duty. We have not.

Real intercession has names in it. Faces. Specific burdens carried before a specific God.

Paul prayed for his churches like a man who knew them. I thank my God every time I remember you, he wrote, and then he prayed particular things, that their love would abound, that they would be filled, that they would stand. So make a list and use it. Move through the directory over a month. Pray for the marriage you know is straining, the teenager drifting, the widow's loneliness, the businessman's pride, the new believer's fragile start. Bring their actual lives before God, the things they told you in confidence and the things you have only guessed. The shepherd who prays for his sheep by name will preach to them differently, sit with them differently, love them differently, because you cannot carry a person's name before God for long without coming to love them.

sections.title: Praying for Them Will Change You First
sections.body:
Something happens to a leader who prays seriously for the people who frustrate him. The critic you cannot stand becomes harder to despise once you have knelt for him.

You cannot hate a man and intercede for him in the same breath for very long. One of them gives.

Intercession is the slow death of a pastor's contempt. The board member who blocks you, the family that left in anger, the one who spread the rumor, all of them soften when you carry them to God instead of carrying them as grievances. Pray for the ones who wronged you, Jesus said, and he did not say it because it changes them, though it may. He said it because it changes you. The bitterness that poisons so many ministries cannot survive an honest prayer life aimed at the very people who caused it. So when someone wounds you, do not first plan your defense. First take their name into the room with God. You will walk out a different shepherd than the one who walked in, and your people will be led by a man whose heart has been kept tender by the only thing that can keep it tender.

sections.title: When You Do Not Know What to Pray
sections.body:
Every praying leader hits the wall where the words run dry and the same tired phrases circle the same tired requests. The answer is not to try harder. It is to borrow better words.

Pray the Scriptures over your people. Let the Bible give your intercession its bones.

When you do not know what to ask for a struggling family, pray Paul's prayers over them, that they would be rooted and grounded in love, strengthened with power in the inner being. Pray the Psalms over the depressed. Pray the promises over the doubting. The Spirit himself, Paul says, intercedes for us when we do not know what to pray, and one of the ways he does it is by giving us the words of God to pray back to God. This also guards your prayers from becoming a list of what you want for the church, which is often just a list of what would make your job easier. Praying Scripture pulls your intercession toward what God actually wills for these people, which is always larger and deeper than your management goals for them.

sections.title: The Sin We Will Not Confess
sections.body:
I have to say the true thing, because if I do not, this whole article is a performance. The reason most of us do not pray for our people is not that we lack time. It is that, somewhere down deep, we think we can do the work without it.

Prayerlessness is not a scheduling problem. It is a confession of self-sufficiency, and it is unbelief in a collar.

We believe in prayer the way we believe in flossing, a good idea we mostly skip, and our ministries run on talent and adrenaline until the talent runs out and the adrenaline turns to dread. The pastor who does not pray is announcing, with his calendar, that he trusts himself more than he trusts God with the souls he was given. I have preached prayer and neglected it in the same week. That is the indictment, and I am inside it. So begin again. Take the list and the chair and the early hour, and do the first work first. Your people do not most need a better strategist or a sharper communicator. They need a shepherd on his knees, holding their names before the only One who can actually keep them. That work is unseen. It is also the only work that lasts.
